title: Claude Fable 5.2 v.s. the Commodore 64: A Turrican-Class Level Game in Two Hours
subtitle: The day after its release, Anthropic’s newest model built an eight-way scrolling C64 platformer in about two hours, drawing every pixel from scratch. The 1982 machine still landed one punch: a bug only a human eye could see.

title: Two Home PCs, One 125B Model: Splitting Strata’s Layers Over Gigabit Ethernet
subtitle: A second PC on a plain network cable made a 4-bit model that did not fit in RAM 87% faster at the same quality. Long prompts got slower, and where one PC was already enough, the second added only power draw.

title: DDR5 Costs Five Times More. My 2013 Workstation Runs a 125B Model Anyway.
subtitle: 38 to 48 tokens per second from a Xeon without AVX2 and two 2017 GPUs, and what three home PCs taught me about where local LLM speed really comes from.

title: When Should a Fast AI Stop and Think?
Laya vs Gemma: Who Wins the Doom Game?
subtitle: A “System One” decision model and a small general-purpose LLM, trained on the same 979 examples, play the same Doom levels on the same GPU. The answer is less exciting than the launch posts, and more useful.

title: OpenAI Says Astra Saturates the Benchmarks. I Gave It 19,656 Cycles Instead.
subtitle: Codex vs. the Commodore 64: a benchmark nobody funded, on a machine nobody can game — and what a 1 MHz CPU says about an agent that a leaderboard cannot.

title: Claude Fable 5.1 Just Shipped. I Made It Scroll a Commodore 64 in Eight Directions at 50 fps.
subtitle: Rung seven of the ladder, measured on release week: banded colour RAM, a raster HUD split and a dozen multiplexed sprites on a 1 MHz CPU — built by an agent that measured before it drew.

title: Dumpster Inference
subtitle: Hardware is declared obsolete against a general-purpose yardstick. Inference is not general purpose. Pick one task, and parts written off years ago come back with most of their value intact — for a third of the money.

title: Qwen3.8–27B on Two Mid-Range GPUs, Measured on Release Day
subtitle: Everyone will publish the benchmark scores. Here is a less glamorous and more useful question: what does it actually cost to run on a home machine — and why that number is not up for negotiation.

title: Muse Glimmer 30B on a Mid-Range Home Build
